newsitem.title: REPUBLIC OF IRELAND: EU summit reaches landmark pact.
newsitem.headline: EU summit reaches landmark pact.

text.p: After a hard-fought battle between France and Germany, European Union leaders Friday agreed on a landmark pact that takes the 15-nation bloc a major step closer to a single currency in 1999.
On the day that European monetary authorities unveiled the future euro banknotes, leaders approved strict limits on the budget deficits of countries that join monetary union.
But in deference to France and other defenders of national sovereignty, they allowed for a political judgment on whether to levy fines on those who overspend.

"This is a victory for Europe. This is a victory for the euro," European Monetary Affairs Commissioner Yves-Thibault de Silguy proclaimed, saying approval of a "Stability and Growth Pact" had sent the right signal to financial markets.

German Finance Minister Theo Waigel, who had pressed for the strictest possible rules of fiscal orthodoxy, told a news conference he was satisfied with the outcome, even though it fell short of the binding, automatic sanctions Bonn had sought.
"The stability pact is a credible signal that the euro will be a hard currency," he said. Asked whether the euro would be as hard as the German mark, Waigel said "Jawohl!" (Yes indeed).

Irish Finance Minister Ruairi Quinn, who chaired the talks that crafted the compromise, said the summit also approved the legal basis of the euro and a mechanism linking it to the currencies of member states that do not immediately join monetary union. That is meant to prevent competitive devaluations that distort trade.

Uncertainty remains over how effective the pact will be in disciplining states that join the EU's planned economic and monetary union. But at a political level, the fact the 15-nation bloc was able to agree to more restrictions on government borrowing is an achievement some observers say merits considerable praise.
"I think to achieve a stability pact at all is a heroic effort," said economist Adrian Schmidt at Chase Manhattan Bank in London.
The summit formally confirmed Dutch central bank governor Wim Duisenberg as head of the European Monetary Institute from next July, succeeding Belgian Alexandre Lamfalussy.
But French President Jacques Chirac said that did not mean Duisenberg would automatically head the future European central bank, which will control monetary policy for the euro.
Symbolically, the EMI unveiled the first euro banknotes, giving millions of Europeans a first glimpse of the currency that will enter their pockets in 2002.

The notes avoid national symbols, landmarks or figures, featuring generic European architectural designs and bridges instead. But they leave space for each member state to add a national symbol if the EU so decides.

When the summit opened Friday morning, Germany, whose citizens are wary of giving up the hard mark for the untried euro, held out for tighter rules defining when countries could be exempted from fines for overspending.

In the end, leaders agreed that countries would be exempted from penalties for running a deficit of more than 3 percent of gross domestic product if their economies shrank by more than 2 percent in a year.
But any fine would be subject to a political judgment if there was a recession of more than 0.75 percent of gross domestic product.
